The Story of Vrushabsen

I bow to Lord Jina, before whom the entire world bows its head with great joy, and I write the story of Vrushabsen.

King Pradyot of Ujjain once rode a maddened elephant into a dense forest for elephant-catching. The elephant carried him far away, running ever forward. He tried hard to stop it but could not. By fortune, the elephant passed under a tree, and a good idea struck him. He caught hold of a branch, hung from it, and slowly lowered himself to the ground. From there he walked to a small but beautiful village called Khet. He sat down at a water-point, terribly thirsty. A girl named Jindatta, daughter of Jinpal, had come to fill water. Seeing his appearance, she recognised him as someone important and gave him water to drink. Afterward, she went home and told her father about Pradyot. Hearing this, Jinpal came running and brought him to his house, where he served him with great honour — bathing and feeding him. Pradyot was very pleased with his hospitality. He revealed his identity to Jinpal, who considered himself most fortunate to have such a great guest. He stayed there some days, and meanwhile his servants arrived to take him back.

One thing should be mentioned: from the moment Pradyot saw Jindatta, he fell deeply in love with her. With Jinpal's consent, he married her. The newlywed couple returned to his kingdom in happiness. Pradyot gave Jindatta the honour of chief queen. Truly, a small gift given at the right time brings great happiness — like a seed sown in the rainy season that bears abundant fruit. Through Jindatta's gift of water to Pradyot, she gained the fortune of becoming a queen.

The new couple began enjoying life together, tasting new pleasures each day. After some time, a son was born to them. On the night the son was to be born, King Pradyot saw a dream of a white bull. This dream, interpreted by his astrologers, indicated that the child would be extraordinarily powerful and virtuous. The child was named Vrushabsen.

Vrushabsen grew up to be handsome, brave, and wise. He studied all the arts and sciences and became a great warrior. When his time came, he succeeded his father as king. He ruled with justice and compassion, following the path of dharma. He worshipped Lord Jina daily, gave generously to the worthy, and protected his subjects with care.

One day, a great monk came to his city and delivered a discourse on the impermanence of worldly life. Vrushabsen's heart was transformed. He realised that despite all his power and wealth, he was still subject to birth, death, and suffering. He renounced his kingdom, took initiation as a monk, and practised intense austerities. Through dedicated spiritual practice, he destroyed his karmas and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that even a small act of kindness — like giving water to a thirsty stranger — can bring extraordinary rewards. Jindatta's simple gift of water led to her becoming a queen. And her son Vrushabsen, despite having all worldly pleasures, recognised their impermanence and found the path to liberation. The wise should practise kindness and detachment.
